statement: Special relativity treats the finite speed of light as a fundamental constraint that gravity must respect.
caveat: Causality language is supplemental when used.

statement: In Newtonian mechanics, inertial mass measures resistance to acceleration through F = ma.
Newtonian gravity uses an inverse-square force proportional to the two masses and appears instantaneous.
Coulomb’s inverse-square law is a static limit of Maxwellian electromagnetism, which is compatible with finite propagation speed.
Gravity cannot simply copy electromagnetism because like masses attract while like charges repel.
caveat: Spin-language is optional and supplemental.

statement: Mass plays the role of gravitational charge, unlike electric charge, which is independent of inertial mass.
Gravitational mass and inertial mass are experimentally equal to very high precision.
caveat: Current precision requires an external citation later.

statement: When gravitational and inertial mass are equal, the test-body mass cancels and gravitational acceleration is universal.
caveat: Assumes the Newtonian test-body setup.

statement: The weak equivalence principle says freely falling test bodies share trajectories when nongravitational effects and self-gravity are negligible.
caveat: States the scope more precisely than the slogan.

statement: Centrifugal force appears in a rotating description but not in the outside inertial description.
Inertial forces necessarily scale with inertial mass.
The equality of inertial and gravitational mass permits Einstein’s hypothesis that gravity is an inertial effect.
A freely falling astronaut feels weightless, while a person supported on Earth feels the support force.
Gravity can be transformed away only locally; tidal relative acceleration remains across an extended region.
caveat: Required limitation of the elevator analogy.

statement: Treating gravity as inertial requires revising which spacetime paths count as straight.
A supported object and a freely falling object trace different paths through a spacetime plot.
A great-circle route can appear curved on a flat map while being the straightest route on the globe.
Free-falling objects follow geodesics in curved spacetime.
A geodesic is locally extremal or straightest motion, not always a globally shortest path.
caveat: Prevents overextending the globe analogy.

statement: Curvature can be detected intrinsically without embedding spacetime in a higher dimension.
caveat: Corrects rubber-sheet intuition.

statement: Einstein needed years to find a mathematical characterization of curved spacetime consistent with his physical insight.
The left side of Einstein’s field equation characterizes spacetime curvature and the right side characterizes matter and energy.
The stress-energy tensor generalizes the Newtonian mass source to relativistic matter and energy.
Stress-energy includes energy density, momentum density, pressure, and stress, not only rest mass.
caveat: Adds components Brown does not enumerate fully.

statement: Matter tells spacetime how to curve, while curved spacetime determines free motion.
caveat: Interpretive slogan, not a literal two-step time process.

statement: The Schwarzschild solution exactly describes spacetime outside a spherically symmetric central mass.
caveat: State the vacuum exterior and symmetry assumptions.

statement: Setting Newtonian escape velocity equal to light speed produces the radius 2GM/c².
The escape-speed calculation is a numerical clue, not the causal derivation of a GR event horizon.
caveat: Essential guardrail.

statement: Slowly lowering a brick extracts gravitational potential energy approximately GMm/r in Newtonian gravity.
Dividing the extracted Newtonian energy by mc² gives the compactness fraction GM/(rc²).
Naively extrapolating the Newtonian fraction can suggest extracting more than the brick’s rest energy.
Recycling such a surplus into new mass would create a perpetual-motion contradiction.
The system forms a black hole before the impossible Newtonian cycle can be completed.
caveat: The exact mechanism is completed in Lesson 6.

statement: An event horizon is a causal boundary whose interior future-directed signals cannot reach the external region.
caveat: Replaces escape-speed language with the GR concept.

statement: The static Schwarzschild description reduces to Newtonian gravity far away and becomes singular for hovering at the horizon.
caveat: Do not apply hovering acceleration to a free-faller.

statement: A static observer near a black hole is accelerated, whereas an orbiting or falling observer can be in free fall.
For static Schwarzschild observers, the clock-rate factor relative to infinity is sqrt(1-2GM/(rc²)).
caveat: Valid outside the horizon for static observers.

statement: Light climbing outward is received at lower frequency and energy because fewer crests arrive per unit time.
A local object with rest energy mc² can have a smaller conserved energy value as measured from infinity.
caveat: Observer and spacetime assumptions must be explicit.

statement: The idealized extractable fraction approaches 1 as the release point approaches the horizon.
caveat: Requires the assumptions in the implementation plan.

statement: An idealized black-hole lowering process can access a much larger fraction of rest energy than chemical or ordinary nuclear reactions.
A distant observer receives increasingly delayed and redshifted signals and does not receive the crossing at finite Schwarzschild time.
caveat: Do not depict a permanently bright frozen image.

statement: The infaller crosses a sufficiently large event horizon in finite proper time without a locally singular event at the horizon.
Tidal forces at the horizon are weaker for larger black holes.
The horizon and curvature singularity are distinct; the horizon can be locally regular while the singularity marks failure of the classical solution.
caveat: Required distinction.

statement: Singularity theorems helped establish black-hole formation as a generic consequence rather than a finely tuned pathology.
caveat: State theorem assumptions later.

statement: Stellar orbits around the Galactic center imply a massive, compact, dark central object.
LIGO observations match signals from compact-object mergers including black-hole binaries.
caveat: Current event counts require later sourcing.

statement: EHT observations resolve emission from matter in strong-gravity environments around supermassive black holes.
caveat: Do not call the bright ring the horizon.

statement: GR predicts deflection of light near the Sun that differs from a simple Newtonian particle estimate.
The 1919 eclipse expeditions reported shifts consistent with Einstein’s prediction and drove his public fame.
caveat: Measurement quality needs historical sourcing.

statement: Confidence in astrophysical black holes comes from converging dynamical, waveform, and imaging evidence.
caveat: Avoid treating one observation as exhaustive proof.

statement: Finite light speed and mass equality are powerful clues but may not uniquely determine GR without more consistency requirements.
When experiments are inaccessible, theory search relies on mathematical consistency and recovery of known limits.
Future AI systems may search not only for results but for human-comprehensible explanations.
caveat: A forecast, not established fact.
